newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia promises foreigners equal T-bill rights.
newsitem.headline: Russia promises foreigners equal T-bill rights.

text.p: Russia will give Russians and non-residents equal treatment on the government securities market by the end of this year, first deputy Central Bank Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko said on Friday.

"Russia has agreed with the International Monetary Fund generally that by the end of 1997 non-residents will receive the full rights which Russian participants in the government securities market now have," he told Reuters Financial Television.
Aleksashenko said the liberalisation would occur in stages.

The Russian authorities opened the government securities market to foreigners last year, and have been gradually easing the terms on which non-residents can buy and trade GKO discount Treasury bills and OFZ government bonds.
Non-residents can open special rouble "S" accounts with designated Russian banks, and buy government securities at auction or in the secondary market with funds transferred to these accounts.
But they can only repatriate funds from these accounts through forward or option deals, currently with a minimum term of two months and four months respectively.

The central bank requires Russian banks offering the "S" accounts to offset a proportion of these forward and option deals with the central bank at special rates, allowing the central bank to influence these rates.
In return the central bank guarantees non-residents who hold securities to maturity a certain dollar yield, though foreigners can earn more than this by trading actively in the secondary market.

The central bank has been reducing this guaranteed yield, which fell to 12.5 from 13.0 percent on January 16. It has also been cutting the minimum term, and the proportion of forward deals which must be offset. This fell on January 16 to 65 from 75 percent.

The Russian authorities have been keen to attract foreign investors to the market, to help fund the cash-strapped government and bring down yields, which have fallen to just over 30 percent from nearly 190 percent in May last year, just before the presidential election.
But they imposed restrictions on movements of capital to avoid a sudden destabilising outflow of funds. The IMF has put pressure on the authorities to eliminate these.

Aleksashenko also said the Federal Securities Commission and the central bank, which had publicly clashed over the role of commercial banks in the equities market, had agreed to let the banks continue to operate on all securities markets.
"Members of the Central Bank, the Federal Securities Commission and the Finance Ministry have resolved most of the ideological disagreements about the future of the securities market," he said.
"A final decision was taken that there will be no limits placed on the activity of credit organisations on the securities market."

The Federal Securities Commission, on whose authority the Central Bank issues licences to trade on securities markets, said in late December that it would stop allowing commercial banks the right to work on the equities market.
The Central Bank publicly opposed the measure. Aleksashenko said it would not be enforced and a new set of regulations would be prepared by October 1, 1997.
